$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ what is the value of $|{v}_{11}|+|{v}_{21}|?$" :question/worked-solution "If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ the columns of $V$ must be the right singular vectors of $A,$ i.e., the unit eigenvectors of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$

From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that the singular values are ${\sigma }_{1}=9$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$ So, the first column of $V$ corresponds to the singular value ${\sigma }_{1}=9.$

Hence, we need to find a unit eigenvector of ${A}^{T}\,A$ that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=81.$ Computing ${A}^{T}\,A-81I,$ we get

$$
{A}^{T}\,A-81I=[\begin{aligned}73 & 24 \\ 24 & 9\end{aligned}]-81[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 24 \\ 24 & -72\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$" :question/worked-solution "Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=16,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-16I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{aligned}]-16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-12 & -6 \\ -6 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ -6 & 13\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ -6 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{8}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m \times m$ matrix, and

$$

![](images/18/18bf28d59138e6c50e950493570a4e9caa8ec2f86eb81d573272cb4677ea1d69.png)

- Since $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix, it represents a scaling along the $x$- and $y$-axes by $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2,$ respectively.

- Since $U$ is again an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix, it represents a rotation, a reflection, or a rotoreflection.

To summarize, we have the following theorem:

17592186045417] [17592186163232 1064 "The **singular value decomposition** (or SVD) of an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is a factorization of the form

$$
A=U \Sigma V^T,
$$

where

- $\Sigma$ is an $m \times n$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $m \times m$ matrix, and

- $V$ is an orthogonal $n \times n$ matrix.

The columns of $U$ are called the **left singular vectors** of $A,$ and the columns of $V$ are called the **right singular vectors** of $A.$

![](images/29/298933eb0a789ebe57a296088172f6927d1573770824c0b0cffb393eb9894c70.svg)

The singular value decomposition of a matrix $A$ can be thought of as a type of diagonalization that works for *any* $m\times n$ matrix!
